title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Xerxes answered: “Artabanus, you reason these matters out reasonably; but do not fear everything, nor weigh each possibility equally. If you set yourself to reckon everything that may happen, weighing it all equally, you would never perform any deed at all. It is better to be of good courage about everything and suffer half the evils that threaten, than to fear everything in advance and suffer nothing at all. If, always arguing against everything that is said, you fail to show the safe course, you earn the same reproach of failure as the man who says the opposite. This, then, is evenly balanced. But how should a mere man know the safe course? I think, in no way. To those who choose to act, gain most often comes; to those who reckon up everything and shrink back, it rarely comes. You see to what great might the power of the Persians has advanced. If the kings who came before me had held opinions like yours, or, without holding them themselves, had had counsellors like you, you would never have seen that power brought forward to this point. As it is, by running risks they brought it here, for great power is generally won by running great risks. We, following their example, are marching now in the finest season of the year; and when we have subdued all Europe, we shall return home, without having met with famine anywhere, or suffering any other unpleasant thing. For we march with great stores of food of our own, and beyond that, we shall have the grain harvests of all the peoples whose lands we come to; and we are marching against men who plow the soil, not against nomad tribes.”
